mitigation_mechanism: Rewetting drained peat — blocking canals so the water table rises — works on the fuel. Restoring closed-canopy forest vegetation on degraded peatland is stated to reduce fire risk through increased moisture in surface and below-ground fire fuels (ev_fire_hazard_mish21_3), and improved hydrology after canal blocking is given as a route to reduced fire hazard (ev_fire_hazard_ritz13_4). Most of the cell describes the hazard from the loss side and the engine reads rewetting as the reversal of that chain: drainage and degradation made peat vulnerable to fire (ev_fire_hazard_bonn16_1); cleared, drained and replanted peat domes become vulnerable to wildfires that, once started, can burn for years (ev_wet_fire_hazard_ramsar18_1); the drier conditions following drainage increase the risk of fire (ev_wgy_ram_14); and in a hotter, drier European climate the risk of forest and peat fires in drained peatlands is expected to increase further (ev_wgy_qa_8). A review of tropical peatland restoration techniques (Dohong et al.) adds that peatland rewetting also provides benefit in terms of reducing fire occurrences caused by dried out peatlands, citing Dohong and Lilia 2008, Page et al. 2009a and Panda et al. 2012 (ev_fire_hazard_doh18_1). The quantified result comes from a modelled fire-hazard index after large-scale canal-blocking rewetting in Riau, Sumatra: the frequency of continuous extreme-class hazard declined by 40% (ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_1). Indonesian project accounts add field observations: in South Sumatra a revegetated project still survived large fires in 2015 and 2019, restoration in the area having restrained the spread of fires from nearby areas (ev_wet_fire_budi20_1); and in Riau 312 canal blocks over 6,060 ha of community land restored the hydrology of the peatland system and reduced the risk of wildfires (ev_wet_fire_terz22_1). Fire frequency and the carbon emitted both rise with proximity to drainage canals in degraded peatland, an effect reported to extend at least 800 m from the canal (ev_fire_hazard_jauhiainen16_5).

mitigation_mechanism: Rewetting raises the water table in the peat, and the water does not stop at the project boundary. The Ramsar technical guidance on peatland rewetting sets two design constraints on this: where adjacent land use may be impaired, rewetting must be done gradually and flooding of surrounding land must be avoided (ev_wgy_ram_15); and where downward seepage is diffuse, elevating the water table in a residual peat massif will require raising the water level in the surrounding land, farmland included (ev_wgy_ram_16). The first treats waterlogging of neighbouring land as a risk to be managed; the second describes a setting where wetting neighbouring farmland is built into the method.
caveats: These are design constraints stated by an authority, not measurements. Neither statement says how often neighbouring land is waterlogged, by how much, for how long, or what it costs the farmers who work it, and both come from one advocacy-adjacent guidance document; they establish that the risk is recognised, not its size or frequency, and they should not be read as evidence that rewetting routinely floods farmland. Unlike the flood benefits elsewhere in this recipe, the cost here falls on the neighbouring farm household rather than downstream. For scoping, a rewetting proposal adjacent to farmland should plan for gradual water-level raising, identify the adjacent parcels whose water level the design may depend on, and treat any need to raise water on those parcels as something to agree with their users before the works, not an incidental side effect. No country, income group, climate zone or farming system is attached to either statement. mitigation_mechanism: Coastal wetland standing between a cyclone and exposed property reduces the damage done, measured as an elasticity across US Atlantic and Gulf coastal counties: a 1% loss of coastal wetlands is associated with a 0.6% increase in property damage (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_1). Valued at the margin, the median county's wetland is worth about $91,000 per km2 per year in storm protection, against an average of about $1.8 million and a range from less than $800 to $100 million per km2 (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_4), and a counterfactual on a single hurricane put the damage attributable to prior wetland loss at about $430 million (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_5). A farm-level observation points the same way: after a cyclone on the Queensland coast, croplands within 1 km of mangroves and tidal marshes showed reduced crop cover declines compared with more distant areas (ev_crop_yield_rowl26w1_2).
caveats: Protection is proportionately smallest where the storm is strongest: the elasticity of property damage with respect to wetlands is 0.58 for a tropical storm and 0.35 for a category 3 to 5 hurricane (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_2, ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_3). Built defences substitute for it — the elasticity is 0.50 in states with stricter building codes against 0.81 where codes and enforcement are weaker (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_6). All of this is measured on existing wetland cover rather than on a restoration project, and the same authors warn that a replacement wetland may take decades to fully develop the functions of the wetland it replaces (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_7), so the measured value is not what a new project delivers. The Queensland result is crop cover read from a satellite vegetation index, not yield, around existing mangrove and marsh that the authors could not separate, and the binary presence of a coastal wetland on the seaward side of a field did not contribute substantially to the models (ev_crop_yield_rowl26w1_3). mitigation_mechanism: Drought damages the restored wetland by taking away the water it runs on. In a rewetted Indonesian peat restoration area, peat-surface subsidence accelerated sharply during and shortly after the 2019 El Niño drought when groundwater depths were very low, running 2.5 to 4 times the rate of the preceding 3.5 years and more than double the 7.5-year mean (ev_climate_shock_hooi24_5). The authors read their long record as showing that a severe drought could still cause major water-table drops to near 1 m below the peat surface, with carbon-emission spikes, even in otherwise rewetted conditions, in restoration areas and remaining peat-swamp forest alike (ev_climate_shock_hooi24_6). On a restored floodplain the hazard works by removing the flood the wetland depends on: in 2020, lack of snow cover and severe drought meant no spring flooding on the Pripyat floodplain, and migrating and nesting birds on the restored floodplain meadows declined strongly (ev_wgy_blr_6). The Ramsar technical guidance records, from its authors' knowledge, that a large number of planted areas in degraded tropical peat-swamp forest have been lost to drought, as well as to fire, flooding and out-competition by ferns and sedges (ev_wgy_ram_22).
caveats: Two of the four units are measurements — subsidence in Sumatra and bird numbers in a Belarus project evaluation; the other two are interpretation: the Hooijer authors' reading of their own record, and an expert statement with no frequency, site or measurement, made where the guidance itself notes there is very little literature on what happens after planting. The Belarus case is floodplain meadow kept open by grazing and mowing, a different wetland type and practice from tropical peat rewetting, and its indicator is birds rather than any livelihood; the evaluation also names drought and snowless winters as arriving faster and more severely than the project was designed for. Settings are upper-middle-income Indonesia and Belarus plus guidance with no site; there is no low-income or lower-middle-income case. Design implication: a wetland investment in a drought-prone setting should budget and monitor for drought-year losses of peat surface, carbon, plantings and habitat function rather than treat them as failure of the works, and should expect the asset to deliver least in the dry years.

The authors read their long record as showing that a severe drought could still cause major water-table drops to near 1 m below the peat surface, with carbon-emission spikes, even in otherwise rewetted conditions, in restoration areas and remaining peat-swamp forest alike (ev_climate_shock_hooi24_6). The Ramsar technical guidance records, from its authors' knowledge, that a large number of planted areas in degraded tropical peat-swamp forest have been lost to drought, as well as to fire, flooding and out-competition by ferns and sedges (ev_wgy_ram_22).
caveats: Only one unit is a measurement, from one Indonesian site; the second Hooijer unit is the authors' reading of their own record, and the Ramsar statement is expert knowledge with no frequency, site or measurement, made where the guidance itself notes there is very little literature on what happens after planting. The cell is humid-tropical peat in an upper-middle-income setting; no temperate peat and no low-income or lower-middle-income site is represented. Design implication: a rewetting investment in drought-prone tropical peat should expect the asset to lose surface elevation and carbon, and plantings to fail, in El Niño years however well the water management performs, and should budget and monitor for that rather than treat it as a failure of the works.

mitigation_mechanism: Drought can switch off the flood pulse a restored floodplain depends on. On a restored floodplain the hazard works by removing the flood the wetland depends on: in 2020, lack of snow cover and severe drought meant no spring flooding on the Pripyat floodplain, and migrating and nesting birds on the restored floodplain meadows declined strongly (ev_wgy_blr_6).
caveats: This is one observation in a project terminal evaluation from Belarus, an upper-middle-income temperate setting, and the practice is restoration and maintenance of open floodplain meadows by grazing and mowing, not rewetting of drained land; the indicator is the number of migrating and nesting birds, not a livelihood or a hydrological measure, and the evaluation gives no size for the decline. It also names drought and snowless winters as arriving faster and more severely than the project was designed for. The lesson that transfers is a design one: a floodplain wetland fed by a seasonal flood is exposed whenever drought removes that flood, so its habitat function, and anything that depends on it, should be expected to fail in such years.

mitigation_mechanism: Flooding can destroy restoration plantings and the structures that keep peat wet. The Ramsar technical guidance records, from its authors' knowledge, that a large number of planted areas in degraded tropical peat-swamp forest have been lost to flooding, as well as to fire, drought and out-competition by ferns and sedges (ev_wgy_ram_21). In South Sumatra, canal blockings were damaged due to flooding in the 2018 wet season, and in the 2019 prolonged dry season the damaged blockings and surrounding open canals lowered the water table in the project area (ev_wet_assetflood_budi20_1). A review of tropical peatland restoration techniques (Dohong et al. 2018) cites a study in Berbak National Park, Jambi, where prolonged and deep flooding in 2004 had killed most of the seedlings planted and the survival rate remained at 5% (van Eijk et al. 2009) [ev_climate_shock_doh18_1].
caveats: The Ramsar line is a single expert statement, with no site, frequency, area or measurement, made where the guidance notes there is very little literature on what happens after planting. It does not say whether the flooding came from rivers or from the raised water table of rewetting itself, and it concerns tropical peat-swamp replanting only. The Berbak figure is the only measured loss rate, reported second-hand from van Eijk et al. at a single national-park site [ev_climate_shock_doh18_1]. Together these are a reason to budget for replanting losses and replacement, not a measured rate of loss. The Sumatran case is a single site on a project its authors describe as never fully rewetted; the sentence is cut by a page break, so the number of damaged blockings is not recoverable. What it does show is the mechanism of loss - flood damage to the dams undoing the rewetting in the following dry season - which argues for budgeting dam inspection and repair after each wet season.

mitigation_mechanism: Storms wear down and tear coastal wetlands in more than one way. A review of storm impacts on coastal wetland elevations (Cahoon) records that high winds combined with storm surge resulted in mangrove forest mortality, defoliation and toppling of trees, in southwest Florida and Guanaja, followed by a post-storm loss of elevation through soil organic matter oxidation [ev_climate_shock_cah06_1]; that in 2002 Hurricane Lili created 257 ha of open water, with a depth of 0.5-1.3 m, at West Cote Blanche, Louisiana, by the lateral movement of the marsh root mat (Barras 2003) [ev_climate_shock_cah06_2]; and that Hurricane Andrew compacted the severely degraded S. alterniflora marsh substrate at Bayou Chitigue by 33 mm in spite of sediment deposition [ev_climate_shock_cah06_3]. A second review, citing a global analysis of salt-marsh erosion and wave measurements, finds that most salt-marsh deterioration is caused by moderate storms of a monthly frequency [ev_erosion_hazard_leon17_6], while intense hurricanes contribute less than 1% to long-term salt-marsh erosion rates [ev_erosion_hazard_leon17_5].
caveats: The class is low: cyclones do damage coastal wetlands, but the condition of the wetland decides how much. The healthy S. alterniflora marsh at Old Oyster Bayou was not compacted by Hurricane Andrew but instead gained elevation equal to the thickness of sediment deposits [ev_climate_shock_cah06_4], against the compaction of the deteriorated marsh nearby [ev_climate_shock_cah06_3] - so a newly planted or degraded site, where the substrate is weakest, is the case to budget for. All the measurements are on existing, established marsh and mangrove on US Gulf and Atlantic coasts and in Honduras, not on restored or created sites [ev_climate_shock_cah06_1, ev_climate_shock_cah06_2], and the erosion analysis is cited second-hand and concerns lateral edge erosion only [ev_erosion_hazard_leon17_5]. A small share of long-term erosion is not a damage rate per event: it is compatible with heavy losses in the year a hurricane does arrive, and edge retreat under the ordinary monthly storm climate is a continuing maintenance cost [ev_erosion_hazard_leon17_6].

mitigation_mechanism: The vulnerable asset is the canal dam that holds the water table up. In December 2005, after an extreme rainfall event, both dams in the Kalampangan Canal were damaged by water seeping underneath and along the sides; they were repaired in March 2006 and were damaged again in August 2006 (ev_climate_shock_ritz13_7). During an extreme rainfall event in August 2007 a further dam was damaged in a flash flood, the canal water level rising by several metres in a short period (ev_climate_shock_ritz13_8). The rainfall is the trigger; the vulnerability is structural, since highly permeable tropical peat lets seepage pass beneath and alongside a dam, and the sunken canals intercept overland and interflow, raising canal discharges when the rain is extreme.
caveats: This is a single demonstration site in Indonesian tropical peat, recorded as a case study rather than measured across projects, and the repeat failure after repair is the most transferable part of it. It says nothing about damage to the wetland itself, about coastal or temperate wetland types, or about water-control structures of other designs. Read it as a design and maintenance risk for canal-blocking programmes in deep permeable peat — dam siting relative to the contour, seepage control, and a repair budget that assumes recurrence — rather than as a general sensitivity of wetland management to extreme rainfall. Provenance: humid-tropical, upper-middle-income, with no comparable record from any other peat region.
